topic: Eigenvectors: the directions a matrix only stretches

segments.narration: What if a matrix could move every single vector in the plane, except a special few?
segments.visual: Title 'Eigenvectors' with the subtitle 'the arrows a matrix can't turn'

segments.narration: A matrix is a transformation machine: feed in any vector, and it outputs a new one.
segments.visual: A box labelled A in the main band with an arrow in (v) and an arrow out (Av)

segments.narration: Here's matrix A. Let's apply it to the whole plane at once and watch.
segments.visual: The matrix A = [[2,1],[1,2]] in the upper band, a coordinate grid in the main band

segments.narration: These two grey arrows get swung around. They point somewhere completely different from where they started.
segments.visual: Two grey arrows on the grid rotate to their transformed positions

segments.narration: Most vectors behave like that: the transformation changes both their length and their direction.
segments.visual: A third grey arrow transforms, also changing direction

segments.narration: But this blue arrow refuses to turn. A only stretches it along its own line.
segments.visual: Grey arrows fade; a blue arrow on the diagonal stretches to triple length along a dashed line

segments.narration: That's an eigenvector. The name comes from German, where eigen means own.
segments.visual: The label 'eigenvector' appears in the lower band

segments.narration: Why doesn't it turn? Because A's push on this vector lines up exactly with the vector itself.
segments.visual: An orange arrow drawn on top of the blue one, showing the push along the same line

segments.narration: In symbols: A times v equals lambda times v. Same direction, just scaled.
segments.visual: The label is replaced by the equation A v = lambda v in the lower band

segments.narration: Lambda is called the eigenvalue. Our arrow stretched to triple length, so lambda equals three.
segments.visual: The equation becomes A v = 3 v and the blue arrow flashes

segments.narration: And hiding on the other diagonal is a second eigenvector, one A doesn't stretch at all.
segments.visual: A green arrow on the anti-diagonal with its own dashed line; it stays the same length

segments.narration: Its eigenvalue is one. Find all the eigenvectors, and you've found the skeleton of the matrix.
segments.visual: The equation becomes lambda one = 3, lambda two = 1

segments.narration: Along these directions a messy transformation becomes simple multiplication. That's why eigenvectors power vibration analysis and PageRank.
segments.visual: Everything fades except the title and the payoff 'the directions a matrix only scales'
